The aggregation order also changes the score: averaging per-prompt percentages gives substantially higher values than taking the percentage of average logit differences.

metrics.name: Pessimistic ROC curve and area under the curve
metrics.caveat: Circuit overlap with a ground truth can be misleading when the ground truth uses a different ablation methodology. The paper compares against ground truths defined using both Zero and Resample Ablations.

confounds.name: The IOI score depends on ablation methodology rather than only on the circuit
confounds.detail: A high faithfulness score could reflect choices such as ablating nodes versus edges, using all versus specified token positions, or using Mean versus Resample Ablation, rather than an invariant property of the circuit.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper reruns IOI evaluations while varying these choices and reports that the resulting faithfulness scores differ substantially; this demonstrates the dependence rather than ruling it out.

confounds.name: The IOI score depends on the prompt subtype
confounds.detail: A pooled score could be driven by the relative performance on ABBA versus BABA prompts rather than uniform faithfulness across the IOI distribution.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper reports the two prompt formats separately and finds systematically higher faithfulness for BABA prompts.

confounds.name: The IOI score depends on the size of the dataset used to compute mean ablations
confounds.detail: The headline score could reflect the number of ABC examples used to estimate the mean activation, rather than just circuit quality.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper varies the ABC dataset size and finds that faithfulness increases monotonically with its size.

confounds.name: The IOI score depends on how per-prompt results are aggregated
confounds.detail: A high score could result from averaging per-prompt percentages instead of computing a percentage from average logit differences.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper computes and compares both aggregation orders, finding substantially higher scores when it averages per-prompt percentages.

confounds.name: An average faithfulness score hides poor performance on individual prompts
confounds.detail: A circuit could match the full model on average while failing on many individual examples, with extreme values balancing one another.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper examines per-prompt scores and reports their spread, including large IQRs and extreme outliers, alongside the average.

evidence_standards.name: Two-sample t-test
evidence_standards.detail: For the Mean-versus-Resample Ablation comparison, the paper reports statistical significance for Node Ablation at p=1e-5, but not for Edge Ablation.

evidence_standards.name: Per-prompt variability reporting
evidence_standards.detail: The paper uses boxplots and reports interquartile ranges and extreme outliers to show variation across prompts; it gives no numerical margin for treating results as equivalent.

datasets.name: MNIST
datasets.eval_protocol: Standard neural-network-verification model; circuits use neuron-level granularity. Input-robustness evaluation uses zero-patching and 100 batches (one circuit per batch), with the input neighborhood set using ε values aligned with VNN-COMP; faithfulness is based on logit difference. The patching-robustness experiment compares zero-patching, mean-patching, and certified continuous-domain patching. No split is specified.

datasets.name: CIFAR-10
datasets.eval_protocol: Standard neural-network-verification model; circuits use convolutional-filter granularity. Input-robustness evaluation uses zero-patching and 100 batches (one circuit per batch), with the input neighborhood set using ε values aligned with VNN-COMP; faithfulness is based on logit difference. The patching-robustness experiment compares zero-patching, mean-patching, and certified continuous-domain patching. No split is specified.

datasets.name: GTSRB
datasets.eval_protocol: Standard neural-network-verification model; circuits use convolutional-filter granularity. Input-robustness evaluation uses zero-patching and 100 batches (one circuit per batch), with the input neighborhood set using ε values aligned with VNN-COMP; faithfulness is based on logit difference. The patching-robustness experiment compares zero-patching, mean-patching, and certified continuous-domain patching. No split is specified.

datasets.name: TaxiNet
datasets.eval_protocol: Standard neural-network-verification model; circuits use convolutional-filter granularity. Input-robustness evaluation uses zero-patching and 100 batches (one circuit per batch), with the input neighborhood set using ε values aligned with VNN-COMP; faithfulness is based on logit difference. The patching-robustness experiment compares zero-patching, mean-patching, and certified continuous-domain patching. No split is specified.

baselines.name: sampling-based circuit discovery
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared as a variant of Algorithm 1 against the provable variant, using the same datasets, model architectures, circuit granularity, logit-difference criterion and tolerance, and zero-patching for the input-robustness experiment.

baselines.name: zero-patching circuit discovery
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared with mean-patching and certified patching-robust discovery using Algorithm 1 and the logit-difference criterion; the resulting circuits are evaluated under the same continuous-domain patching-robustness criterion.

baselines.name: mean-patching circuit discovery
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared with zero-patching and certified patching-robust discovery using Algorithm 1 and the logit-difference criterion; the resulting circuits are evaluated under the same continuous-domain patching-robustness criterion.

metrics.name: logit difference
metrics.caveat: A bound assessed only on sampled inputs may fail under continuous input perturbations; the paper also reports certified robustness over the continuous input domain.

metrics.name: robustness (%)
metrics.caveat: Sampling-based or fixed-patching robustness can miss failures elsewhere in the continuous input or patching domain; the paper reports the certified continuous-domain result alongside the standard-condition results.

metrics.name: circuit size (|C|)
metrics.caveat: Smaller size alone does not establish global cardinal minimality; the paper distinguishes several minimality notions and reports MHS size as a lower bound, with circuit size for comparison.

metrics.name: MHS size
metrics.caveat: It lower-bounds the cardinally minimal circuit size and is not necessarily the size of a faithful circuit; the paper compares it with discovered circuit size and reports when the bound is met.

confounds.name: The certified method’s stronger robustness could result from producing larger circuits
confounds.detail: Larger circuits might preserve model behavior more readily, making robustness gains appear to support certification rather than the method’s guarantees.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper reports comparable circuit sizes for sampling-based and provably input-robust circuits, and describes the certified patching-robust circuits as achieving stronger robustness at comparable sizes.

confounds.name: Standard-patching circuits could appear less robust because they are assessed under a different criterion
confounds.detail: A difference in evaluation criteria could explain the reported robustness gap without showing that standard-patching circuits fail under perturbations.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Circuits found with zero or mean patching are evaluated under the same continuous-domain criterion as the certified patching setting.

evidence_standards.name: 100 batches for input-robustness results
evidence_standards.detail: The paper reports one circuit per batch and presents results as values with ± dispersion; it does not specify the dispersion type, seeds, or a statistical test.

evidence_standards.name: Convergence comparison over time
evidence_standards.detail: Circuit-size convergence is shown over the first 10 minutes, with the shaded region described as deviation; the paper does not state a statistical test or a numerical margin for calling differences real.

datasets.name: transformersbook/codeparrot
datasets.eval_protocol: Primary fine-tuning corpus, streamed for 500K tokens. Runs use seeds 42, 123, and 7, with checkpoints at steps 0, 100, and 200. At each checkpoint, the induction score is measured on 500 repeated-token sequences with half-length 50. No train/test split is specified.

datasets.name: roneneldan/TinyStories
datasets.eval_protocol: Prose fine-tuning control, using the same 500K-token budget, seeds, and checkpoint schedule as the code condition. At each checkpoint, the induction score is measured on 500 repeated-token sequences with half-length 50. No train/test split is specified.

baselines.name: Pretrained attn-only-2l checkpoint
baselines.fair_comparison: The code and prose fine-tuning conditions start from the same pretrained model; the paper compares their checkpoint scores with the step-0 score. No separate baseline hyperparameter tuning is described.

metrics.name: Prefix-matching score (induction score, IS)
metrics.caveat: An initially used off-by-one formula measured attention to the first occurrence itself and gave misleading near-zero scores; the corrected formula measures attention to the token following that occurrence. The paper says the IS threshold of 0.5 is only a visualization reference, not a hard criterion; activation-patching attribution is also reported.

metrics.name: Activation-patching attribution (Attr)
metrics.caveat: The circuit-membership threshold of 0.5 is arbitrary; the paper reports raw attribution values as well. Only L1H6 exceeds the threshold, and the authors note that the missing layer-0 partner may reflect the threshold or pooled corruption.

metrics.name: Normalized logit difference on adversarial probes
metrics.caveat: The all-same-token probe is a normalization artefact because every position trivially satisfies the prefix-matching criterion; the paper says its large value should not be interpreted as super-induction. Probe-category results are reported alongside it.

controls.name: TinyStories prose fine-tuning control
controls.detail: Fine-tunes the same pretrained model on 500K tokens of prose, with the same three seeds and checkpoint schedule as code fine-tuning.
controls.rules_out: That the observed increase is specific to code only by comparison with another fine-tuning corpus; it permits a comparison of reinforcement magnitude across these two domains.

controls.name: Pretrained step-0 model
controls.detail: The unmodified pretrained attn-only-2l model is measured before fine-tuning and used as the reference for changes in both fine-tuning conditions.
controls.rules_out: That the reported score increase is merely a difference between unrelated starting checkpoints.

controls.name: Structure-preserving adversarial probes
controls.detail: Post-fine-tuning probes that preserve induction structure, including substitutions and clean repeated sequences; compared with the clean score and structure-removing probes.
controls.rules_out: Together with structure-removing probes, tests whether the high post-fine-tuning score is selective for induction structure rather than a generic response to perturbations.

controls.name: Structure-removing adversarial probes
controls.detail: Post-fine-tuning probes that disrupt induction structure, including reversing the second half, cyclic shifts, and fully random sequences; compared with structure-preserving probes.
controls.rules_out: Together with structure-preserving probes, tests whether the high post-fine-tuning score is selective for induction structure rather than a generic high-attention effect.

controls.name: Second-half-shuffled corrupted run
controls.detail: For activation patching, the second half of each repeated-token sequence is randomly shuffled; a head output from the clean run is patched into this corrupted run.
controls.rules_out: Tests whether the patched head contributes causally to recovery of the target behavior relative to the corrupted run.

confounds.name: The post-fine-tuning score increase is a generic high-attention effect rather than stronger selective induction
confounds.detail: A broad increase in attention could produce a higher prefix-matching score without the head becoming more selective for induction structure.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Post-fine-tuning structure-preserving probes retain a mean score of 0.944, while structure-removing probes fall to 0.132; the paper interprets this contrast as evidence against a generic high-attention artefact.

confounds.name: The near-zero induction score reflects the model rather than a scoring implementation error
confounds.detail: The early off-by-one implementation produced near-zero prefix-matching scores, which could have been mistaken for absence of the induction head.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The authors corrected the index to attend to the token following the first occurrence; the resulting L1H6 score was 0.408, consistent with its independently measured activation-patching attribution of 0.952. They also tested the suspected BOS-prepending issue and report no measurable effect.

confounds.name: The code-versus-prose difference is a seed artefact
confounds.detail: The reported domain-dependent gap could result from a particular random initialization or run rather than the fine-tuning corpus.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The authors report results across seeds 42, 123, and 7, with inter-seed standard deviations no greater than 0.007, and say the code-versus-prose result is unlikely to be a seed artefact; they acknowledge that three seeds are modest and do not treat the gap as fully established.

evidence_standards.name: Three random seeds; mean ± standard deviation
evidence_standards.detail: The main trajectories are reported across seeds 42, 123, and 7 as mean ± SD. The authors acknowledge that three seeds are modest and suggest five or more would better establish the code-versus-prose gap.

evidence_standards.name: A priori practical-change threshold for IS
evidence_standards.detail: An IS change of at least 0.1 is treated as practically meaningful. The paper reports the threshold as a priori and not adjusted post hoc.

evidence_standards.name: Code-versus-prose separation judged against pooled standard deviation
evidence_standards.detail: At step 200, the reported gap is +0.030, or 4.1× the pooled SD, and is described as statistically meaningful. At step 100, the gap is 1.5× the pooled SD and is described as suggestive but not conclusive; no formal statistical test is specified.

datasets.name: Indirect Object Identification (IOI)
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluated as a circuit-level task suite: the primary evaluation includes one task circuit for each of 3 models; the scaled evaluation uses 3 circuits from disjoint prompt subsets per model. Circuits are extracted with EAP-IG retaining k=200 edges and assessed for task accuracy and causal contribution.

datasets.name: Location semantic-role binding
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluated as a circuit-level task suite: the primary evaluation includes one task circuit for each of 3 models; the scaled evaluation uses 3 circuits from disjoint prompt subsets per model. Circuits are extracted with EAP-IG retaining k=200 edges and assessed for task accuracy and causal contribution.

datasets.name: Time semantic-role binding
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluated as a circuit-level task suite: the primary evaluation includes one task circuit for each of 3 models; the scaled evaluation uses 3 circuits from disjoint prompt subsets per model. Circuits are extracted with EAP-IG retaining k=200 edges and assessed for task accuracy and causal contribution.

datasets.name: Path semantic-role binding
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluated as a circuit-level task suite: the primary evaluation includes one task circuit for each of 3 models; the scaled evaluation uses 3 circuits from disjoint prompt subsets per model. Circuits are extracted with EAP-IG retaining k=200 edges and assessed for task accuracy and causal contribution.

datasets.name: Greater-Than (GT)
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluated as a circuit-level task suite: the primary evaluation includes one task circuit for each of 3 models; the scaled evaluation uses 3 circuits from disjoint prompt subsets per model. Circuits are extracted with EAP-IG retaining k=200 edges and assessed for task accuracy and causal contribution.

baselines.name: Random forest
baselines.fair_comparison: Trained on the same structural features used as ILP background knowledge.

baselines.name: Euclidean distance over feature vectors
baselines.fair_comparison: Uses the same feature vectors as the ILP structural features.

metrics.name: Direct Logit Attribution (DLA), δv
metrics.caveat: Individual components can all fall below the marginality cutoff even when the circuit has substantial causal relevance; the LLaMA IOI circuit has 29 marginal components despite ΔT=5.24.

metrics.name: Attribution-weighted attention profile (πv) and dominant linguistic-role proportion
Causal contribution, ΔT
metrics.caveat: The paper says cross-model comparisons are unreliable when a circuit's ΔT is near zero, citing Time's Pythia-1B value of 0.003.

metrics.name: One-vs-rest F1
metrics.caveat: Used to select clauses; ties are resolved in favour of shorter clauses.

metrics.name: ILP signature distance
metrics.caveat: Similar distances can group circuits with different computations: GT clusters with semantic-role circuits because their clauses share predicate vocabulary.

metrics.name: Random-forest leave-one-out accuracy
metrics.caveat: The reported 60% accuracy misclassifies GT and IOI; the paper contrasts this with the inspectable clauses provided by ILP.

metrics.name: Node Jaccard overlap
metrics.caveat: Raw component overlap is near zero across model pairs, so it does not support transfer by node identity.

controls.name: Size-matched random circuits
controls.detail: Evaluated 50 size-matched random circuits per task across the two Pythia models; the reported evaluated sets contain 34 circuits on Pythia-14M and 35 on Pythia-1B, including multi-split variants.
controls.rules_out: That the causal contribution of discovered circuits is explained by chance subgraphs or circuit size alone.

controls.name: Blind structural-predicate clause search (Pool B)
controls.detail: Alongside clauses using named motifs in Pool A, the paper searches clauses using blind structural predicates such as edge-type patterns, layer-span, and component-composition predicates.
controls.rules_out: That learned structural signatures depend only on the hand-defined motif names.

controls.name: Unablated full model
controls.detail: Task accuracy on the intact model M is compared with accuracy after ablating circuit C to calculate ΔT; intact-model accuracy is also used in the normalised faithfulness definition.
controls.rules_out: That the reported causal contribution is just the ablated model's score without reference to the intact model.

confounds.name: The circuit effect is due to chance structure or size rather than a causally relevant circuit
confounds.detail: A positive causal contribution could also arise from an arbitrary subgraph of comparable size.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Evaluate size-matched random circuits; they yield ΔT approximately 0, while real circuits outperform them in 29/34 Pythia-14M cases and 28/35 Pythia-1B cases (p<0.05).

confounds.name: Structural signatures work only because of hand-defined motif names
confounds.detail: Apparent structural separation could be an artefact of the named motifs supplied to the learner.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Also search Pool B clauses using blind structural predicates rather than named motifs; the paper describes this as a check that signatures are not limited to hand-defined motif names.

confounds.name: A structural match alone is being mistaken for transfer of the same mechanism
confounds.detail: A retrieved candidate could match the source signature structurally without supporting the target behaviour or having causal relevance.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Screen retrieved target candidates with behavioural and causal validation; the paper explicitly treats structural retrieval as a proposal, not proof of mechanism identity.

confounds.name: Transfer candidate selection is driven by source-circuit behaviour rather than the structural signature
confounds.detail: Different source causal-contribution values could otherwise account for which target candidates are accepted.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The accept/reject pattern is identical across the two transfer directions despite very different source ΔT values; the paper reports this as evidence that structural signatures drive candidate selection.

evidence_standards.name: Permutation test for CFS task-family clustering
evidence_standards.detail: Reports p=0.008 for clustering by task family on Pythia-1B.

evidence_standards.name: Random-circuit comparison
evidence_standards.detail: Uses 34 evaluated random-circuit cases on Pythia-14M and 35 on Pythia-1B; real circuits are better in 29/34 and 28/35 cases, respectively, with p<0.05.

evidence_standards.name: ILP signature-distance matching threshold
evidence_standards.detail: Uses δILP=0.30 as the separation and candidate-matching threshold; the paper says thresholds are empirically chosen and sensitivity analysis confirms stability across the primary range.

baselines.name: Std (standard IRN training)
baselines.fair_comparison: Used as a baseline when fine-tuning OpenAI’s GPT-2 SAE; evaluated with the same verification setup as Sec. 4.

baselines.name: PGD adversarial training
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared as a GPT-2 SAE fine-tuning regime; evaluated with the same verification setup as Sec. 4.

baselines.name: LoRA
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared as a GPT-2 SAE fine-tuning regime; evaluated with the same verification setup as Sec. 4.

metrics.name: Top-20 Jaccard index of active feature sets
metrics.caveat: An attack witnesses only one bad input, so its result is an upper bound on the true worst-case overlap and cannot exclude a lower value; the paper reports attack-derived upper bounds alongside certified lower bounds.

metrics.name: Faithfulness gap (maximum ℓ∞ difference, bounded by δ)
metrics.caveat: The exact worst-case gap is generally infeasible to compute; the paper brackets it with an attack-derived lower bound and a verified upper bound.

metrics.name: Next-token prediction flip rate under minor paraphrases

controls.name: Standard-trained GPT-2 SAE (Std)
controls.detail: The given OpenAI GPT-2 SAE obtained using standard training, compared alongside the alternative fine-tuning regimes.
controls.rules_out: That the faithfulness improvement is merely due to using a fine-tuned IRN rather than verification-aware training.

confounds.name: Feature changes reflect fragility of the underlying model, not just IRN unfaithfulness
confounds.detail: The underlying model may itself behave differently on a semantically equivalent paraphrase, so changed active features need not by themselves show that the IRN misrepresents the model’s computation.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Not ruled out: the paper measures next-token prediction changes and reports that GPT-2 flips its prediction for 21% of minor paraphrases; it identifies underlying-model fragility as a contributor to the feature-overlap results.

confounds.name: The measured faithfulness gap is an artifact of an incomplete verifier
confounds.detail: An incomplete verifier could produce loose upper bounds that make the IRN appear less faithful than it is.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper also obtains attack-derived lower bounds on the difference, and reports that these rise along with the verified upper bounds.

evidence_standards.name: Formal bounds with distribution summaries
evidence_standards.detail: For the faithfulness gap, the paper uses attack-derived lower bounds and verified upper bounds, reporting their medians and 25th/75th quantiles. For feature overlap, it reports certified lower bounds and attack-derived upper bounds over test samples, with the 25th percentile of the lower bounds and 75th percentile of the upper bounds as whiskers.

datasets.name: ChatGPT-generated suggestion questions
datasets.eval_protocol: 20 questions asking for suggestions on how to respond to situations; inject the dishonesty direction at layer 15 and assess whether the model is steered toward dishonesty. The paper reports steering on all 20 and consistent dishonest continuation over a long generation horizon.

datasets.name: Truthfulness test datapoints
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluate linear truthfulness directions in Llama-2-7B-chat using accuracy; the paper reports 95.05%. The test-set size and other protocol details are not stated.

metrics.name: Token log probabilities and log-probability differences

controls.name: Model run without dishonesty injection
controls.detail: The paper compares outputs and token log probabilities with and without the layer-15 dishonesty-direction injection; it also uses the no-injection run as the corrupted run in activation patching and uses α=0 as the no-injection reference for direct logit attribution.
controls.rules_out: Shows whether the reported steering and changes in token probabilities or patching outcomes differ from the model’s unmodified behavior.

confounds.name: The direction merely boosts generically dishonest tokens
confounds.detail: The apparent steering effect could arise from directly increasing the probability of a generic set of dishonest tokens, rather than from a meaningful representation.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Directly unembed the layer-15 dishonesty direction and inspect the resulting token distribution; the paper reports relatively high entropy and seemingly arbitrary top tokens.

confounds.name: A first-token shift alone is sufficient for open-ended dishonest generation
confounds.detail: The injection could change only the first token, with that change then causing the rest of the response to be dishonest even without continued intervention.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Compare output log probabilities across token positions with and without injection; the paper concludes that continual dishonesty injections are required along the generation.

baselines.name: ReLU autoencoders
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared with TopK at fixed numbers of latents and, in separate comparisons, fixed sparsity; non-TopK results at fixed L0 are interpolated in log-log space.

baselines.name: ProLU autoencoders
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared with TopK and other activation functions at fixed numbers of latents and at fixed L0 in separate comparisons; non-TopK results at fixed L0 are interpolated in log-log space.

baselines.name: Gated sparse autoencoders
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared with TopK and other activation functions at fixed numbers of latents and at fixed L0 in separate comparisons.

baselines.name: residual stream channels
baselines.fair_comparison: Used as a baseline for probe scores; the paper does not specify further matching details.

baselines.name: zero-ablation baseline
baselines.fair_comparison: The loss from ablating activations to zero is used as a reference for the fraction-of-loss-recovered fidelity metric; the paper does not specify further matching details.

baselines.name: bigrams
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared with N2G explanations of autoencoder latents for downstream loss; the paper does not specify further matching details.

metrics.name: L0 (number of active latents)
metrics.caveat: The reconstruction-sparsity frontier is not the ultimate goal and can favor structureless solutions; behavior and feature-quality metrics are also evaluated. Latents become dense as L0 approaches d_model.

metrics.name: normalized reconstruction MSE
metrics.caveat: Comparing MSE across different numbers of latents is not a fair comparison because larger autoencoders have a looser information bottleneck; the paper also evaluates downstream loss and feature-quality metrics. MSE is normalized by the error from always predicting mean activations.

metrics.name: downstream KL divergence
metrics.caveat: Raw loss numbers are difficult to interpret in absolute terms; the paper also reports delta cross-entropy and relates downstream loss to the pretraining compute of a language model with comparable loss.

metrics.name: delta cross-entropy
metrics.caveat: Raw loss numbers are difficult to interpret in absolute terms; delta cross-entropy is measured relative to the perfect-autoencoder cross-entropy, and the paper also gives a pretraining-compute interpretation.

metrics.name: relative pretraining compute for comparable downstream loss
metrics.caveat: The paper presents this as a more natural absolute interpretation than fidelity relative to zero ablation, which can give high scores even when behavior is poorly explained.

metrics.name: 1d probe loss
metrics.caveat: It relies on strong assumptions about which features are natural; the authors also report that the metric is noisy and say broader, higher-quality tasks could improve it.

metrics.name: N2G explanation precision, recall, and F1
metrics.caveat: Recall alone can reward overly broad explanations with poor precision, so precision and recall are considered together. These metrics binarize activations, making dense token patterns trivially easy to explain; the paper also evaluates simulated explanations by downstream loss.

metrics.name: N2G explanation reconstruction downstream loss
metrics.caveat: The paper uses this simulated-value measure alongside binarized precision/recall metrics; N2G itself captures only simple n-gram-with-wildcard patterns.

metrics.name: ablation sparsity ((L1/L2)^2, normalized by V·T)
metrics.caveat: A constant difference across logits does not affect post-softmax probabilities, so the paper subtracts the median logit difference at each token before computing the measure.

metrics.name: dead-latent fraction
metrics.caveat: A latent is counted as dead if it has not activated in 10 million tokens when no mitigations are applied.

controls.name: training without dead-latent mitigations
controls.detail: The paper reports ablations without the dead-latent mitigations, alongside its recipe using encoder initialization from the decoder transpose and an auxiliary loss using top-k_aux dead latents.
controls.rules_out: That the low dead-latent rate is obtained without the stated mitigations; the paper reports up to 90% dead latents in ablations and 7% in its largest autoencoder with the techniques.

confounds.name: lower MSE with more latents reflects a looser information bottleneck rather than better features
confounds.detail: Larger autoencoders can achieve lower reconstruction error because their latents have a looser information bottleneck, so MSE across different widths alone could make scaling look like improved autoencoder quality.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper evaluates downstream language-model loss and feature-quality measures, including probes, explanations, and ablation sparsity, in addition to MSE.

confounds.name: high zero-ablation fidelity reflects catastrophic loss from zeroing the residual stream, not good behavioral explanation
confounds.detail: Because ablating the residual stream to zero causes very high downstream loss, even a poor explanation can recover a high fraction of that loss.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper reports delta cross-entropy relative to a perfect autoencoder and proposes interpreting downstream loss via the pretraining compute needed for comparable language-model loss; it notes the 16M model's zero-ablation fidelity is 98.2%.

confounds.name: an explanation score is high because the explanation is broad and has poor precision
confounds.detail: An explanation that activates on a broader pattern can have high recall despite failing to capture the specific feature; the paper gives the example of explaining a feature for “don’t stop” or “can’t stop” with all instances of “stop.”
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper evaluates N2G explanation precision as well as recall and F1.

confounds.name: N2G explanations look easy because dense activation patterns are trivial to explain
confounds.detail: The paper notes that dense token patterns are trivial to explain and that some autoencoders have very dense latents.
confounds.ruled_out_by: It also evaluates simulated N2G explanation values by their downstream loss after decoding, a measure the authors say addresses the binarized-metric issue.

confounds.name: the TopK advantage over ReLU is due to activation shrinkage from the L1 penalty
confounds.detail: ReLU models may have worse reconstruction because the L1 penalty shrinks positive activations, rather than because of another property of the activation method.
confounds.ruled_out_by: With the decoder and sparsity mask fixed, the paper optimizes only the nonzero activation values under a positivity constraint. Refinement increases ReLU activations more than TopK activations, but closes only part of the performance gap.

confounds.name: probe scores fail to capture feature quality because the selected tasks assume particular features are natural
confounds.detail: The probe metric depends on strong assumptions about which features an autoencoder should recover; the authors also acknowledge that it is noisy.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Not ruled out; the paper acknowledges this limitation and suggests broader and higher-quality tasks.

datasets.name: sparse probing
datasets.eval_protocol: Run k-sparse logistic-regression probes on SAE latents across 5 probing datasets; report top-k accuracy. On the synthetic panel, use 92 binary tasks, with class-balanced samples, up to 1,024 training and 3,000 test activations per task.

datasets.name: sae-probes sparse probing
datasets.eval_protocol: Run L1-regularized logistic-regression probes with cross-validation across 113 datasets; report accuracy. Reseed-noise results include k=1 and k=5.

datasets.name: Spurious Correlation Removal (SCR)
datasets.eval_protocol: Run on 2 datasets. Train biased probes on co-occurring concepts, then ablate the top-N SAE latents associated with the spurious attribute and measure bias removal. On the synthetic panel, use 9–12 (T,S) pairs per seed, balanced samples across six classes, and an 80/20 train/test split.

datasets.name: Targeted Probe Perturbation (TPP)
datasets.eval_protocol: Run on 2 datasets. Train probes for classes within a category, ablate the top-N latents most damaging to the focal-class probe, and measure the damage gap between that probe and unrelated probes. On the synthetic panel, use 60 four-sibling groups, with an 80/20 train/test split.

datasets.name: Autointerp
datasets.eval_protocol: Randomly select N SAE latents, have an LLM generate labels, then have a second LLM predict whether each latent fires on held-out explanations. The paper evaluates it on SAE panels but does not specify a split or trial count here.

datasets.name: RAVEL
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluate disentanglement, causal effect, and isolation for latents corresponding to known relational properties, using SAE latents to change predicted attributes for target entities without affecting related entities. The paper evaluates it on SAE panels but does not specify a split or trial count here.

datasets.name: SynthSAEBench-16k synthetic task suite
datasets.eval_protocol: Train width-4,096 SAEs on 200M synthetic samples. For each task, draw a fresh 60,000-activation pool per task-generation seed, balance positive and negative classes, and use an 80/20 train/test split where applicable. Sparse probing uses 92 tasks; TPP uses 60 four-sibling groups; SCR uses 9–12 (T,S) pairs per seed. Compare proxy scores with GT-MCC and GT-F1.

metrics.name: sparse-probing top-k accuracy
metrics.caveat: At canonical top-k=16, single in-sae feature accuracy exceeds 0.99 for almost every trained SAE despite GT-MCC spanning 0.56–0.79, so the score saturates and poorly separates high-quality SAEs; the paper reports correlations with GT-MCC and GT-F1 alongside it.

metrics.name: sae-probes accuracy
metrics.caveat: It struggles to separate variants of the same SAE architecture; the paper compares its between-variant signal with training-seed and snapshot noise.

metrics.name: TPP score
metrics.caveat: At canonical top-N=10 it has essentially zero correlation with GT-MCC; at top-N≥50 it declines through training. The paper reports correlations with GT-MCC and GT-F1 and training trajectories alongside it.

metrics.name: SCR score
metrics.caveat: It can decline during training, rank a perfect oracle below trained SAEs, and become negatively correlated with ground truth at large top-N. The paper reports GT-MCC and GT-F1 correlations and training trajectories alongside it.

metrics.name: Autointerp score
metrics.caveat: Its reseed noise is reported as 0.5% CV on the canonical SAE; it cannot be checked against synthetic ground truth because it requires natural-language concepts.

metrics.name: RAVEL disentangle score
metrics.caveat: It has low reseed noise but only a real, small between-variant signal on the Matryoshka panel; the paper reports reseed noise and variant/seed/snapshot variance alongside it.

metrics.name: RAVEL cause score
metrics.caveat: It has 2.8% reseed CV and is among the metrics whose seed or snapshot noise can dominate variant differences; the paper reports reseed noise and variance decomposition alongside it.

metrics.name: GT-MCC
metrics.caveat: GT-MCC and GT-F1 capture different aspects of SAE quality and do not always peak at the same L0; the paper uses both as ground-truth measures.

metrics.name: GT-F1
metrics.caveat: GT-F1 and GT-MCC capture different aspects of SAE quality and do not always peak at the same L0; the paper uses both as ground-truth measures.

metrics.name: Mean Squared Error (MSE)
metrics.caveat: Used as a core reconstruction reference; the paper finds clearer separation and stability for MSE than for the non-core quality metrics.

metrics.name: coefficient of variation (CV)
metrics.caveat: Low reseed noise alone does not establish that a metric measures SAE quality; the paper also checks ground-truth correlation and discriminability.

metrics.name: minimum-reliable difference |Δ|*
metrics.caveat: For two single-seed scores, differences below the stated threshold are not reliable at the paper’s 95% two-tailed criterion; the paper reports the threshold alongside score means and standard deviations.

metrics.name: Spearman ρ
metrics.caveat: Metric rankings agree more when SAEs are very different than when they are similar; the paper reports cross-metric ranking agreement separately for the cross-architecture and Matryoshka panels.

controls.name: random_init control SAE
controls.detail: A degraded variant of the canonical JumpReLU L0=25 SAE with randomized weights.
controls.rules_out: If a proxy distinguishes it from trained SAEs, that supports sensitivity to learned SAE structure rather than merely returning a score for an SAE-shaped object.

controls.name: random_l0_matched control SAE
controls.detail: A degraded variant with randomized weights and threshold tuned to L0≈25.
controls.rules_out: Tests whether proxy behavior is explained by matching sparsity alone rather than learned structure.

controls.name: permuted_decoder control SAE
controls.detail: A degraded variant of the canonical JumpReLU L0=25 SAE with shuffled decoder rows.
controls.rules_out: Tests whether proxy behavior depends on the decoder’s feature alignment.

controls.name: perfect-oracle SAE
controls.detail: Its decoder is the first 4,096 ground-truth feature directions and its encoder returns exact ground-truth activations; GT-MCC=GT-F1=1 by construction.
controls.rules_out: Tests whether a proxy assigns an appropriate score to a known-perfect SAE; the paper reports that SCR at top-N=10 scores this oracle below 11 trained SAEs.

controls.name: out-of-sae synthetic tasks
controls.detail: Negative-control probing and TPP tasks target features outside the first 4,096 features represented by the width-4,096 SAE; sparse probing also includes out-of-sae and mixed-feature task categories.
controls.rules_out: Tests whether a proxy score tracks SAE quality when the task concerns features the SAE is not explicitly tracking.

confounds.name: A repeatable metric may measure something other than SAE quality
confounds.detail: Low reseed noise and discriminability could still arise from an arbitrary, repeatable function of SAE latents.
confounds.ruled_out_by: On synthetic SAEs with computable ground truth, correlate proxy scores with both GT-MCC and GT-F1.

confounds.name: TPP may track out-of-sae feature mixing rather than SAE quality
confounds.detail: TPP’s correlation with out-of-sae features could make its score look meaningful without measuring recovery of features represented by the SAE.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Partition synthetic tasks into in-sae and out-of-sae groups and measure correlations with GT-MCC and GT-F1; the paper finds TPP can correlate better with out-of-sae features and does not establish it as a reliable quality proxy.

confounds.name: Apparent differences between SAE variants may be training-seed or snapshot noise
confounds.detail: A single panel run could name a winner even if the score variation comes from seed randomness or checkpoint jitter rather than the variant.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Train three seeds per Matryoshka variant, evaluate ten post-warmup snapshots per run, and decompose score variance into variant, training-seed, and snapshot components.

confounds.name: Synthetic-panel results may not establish proxy correctness on real LLMs
confounds.detail: The authors concede that biases or dataset limitations may remain undetected without ground truth on real LLMs.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Not ruled out in this paper; the authors state that synthetic ground-truth tests cannot establish with certainty that a proxy is correct on LLMs.

evidence_standards.name: Five reseeds and a 95% two-tailed minimum-reliable-difference threshold
evidence_standards.detail: Run each evaluation five times with different random seeds on the same fixed SAE, disabling activation caching. Report mean, standard deviation, and CV. For comparing two single-seed scores, compute |Δ|*=t_(0.025,4)·s√2≈3.93s; differences smaller than this are not reliable under that criterion.

evidence_standards.name: Three training seeds and ten post-warmup snapshots per Matryoshka variant
evidence_standards.detail: Report seed means and min/max envelopes, and decompose variance into between-variant, training-seed, and snapshot components. The paper uses SNR≥1 for the cross-metric ranking analysis and assesses whether between-variant signal is distinguishable from chance.

datasets.name: WMDP-bio
datasets.eval_protocol: Use biology-related text from the corpus as the forget set; measure unlearning by degraded accuracy on WMDP-bio test questions. No split or trial count is specified.

datasets.name: WikiText
datasets.eval_protocol: Use as the retain set when comparing activation frequencies with the WMDP-bio forget set. No split or trial count is specified.

datasets.name: MMLU
datasets.eval_protocol: Use MMLU categories to verify retained capabilities after unlearning. No categories, split, or trial count are specified.

baselines.name: ReLU SAE
baselines.fair_comparison: Main architecture comparisons use 65k-width SAEs on Gemma-2-2B and compare across L0 values; the paper says SAEs were trained using the same library, but does not specify matched hyperparameters.

baselines.name: MatryoshkaBatchTopK SAE
baselines.fair_comparison: Main architecture comparisons use 65k-width SAEs on Gemma-2-2B and compare across L0 values; the paper says SAEs were trained using the same library, but does not specify matched hyperparameters.

baselines.name: TopK SAE
baselines.fair_comparison: Main architecture comparisons use 65k-width SAEs on Gemma-2-2B and compare across L0 values; the paper says SAEs were trained using the same library, but does not specify matched hyperparameters.

baselines.name: BatchTopK SAE
baselines.fair_comparison: Main architecture comparisons use 65k-width SAEs on Gemma-2-2B and compare across L0 values; the paper says SAEs were trained using the same library, but does not specify matched hyperparameters.

baselines.name: Gated SAE
baselines.fair_comparison: Main architecture comparisons use 65k-width SAEs on Gemma-2-2B and compare across L0 values; the paper says SAEs were trained using the same library, but does not specify matched hyperparameters.

baselines.name: JumpReLU SAE
baselines.fair_comparison: Main architecture comparisons use 65k-width SAEs on Gemma-2-2B and compare across L0 values; the paper says SAEs were trained using the same library, but does not specify matched hyperparameters.

baselines.name: P-Annealing SAE
baselines.fair_comparison: Main architecture comparisons use 65k-width SAEs on Gemma-2-2B and compare across L0 values; the paper says SAEs were trained using the same library, but does not specify matched hyperparameters.

baselines.name: Probing directly on K residual-stream channels

metrics.name: Loss Recovered / sparsity–fidelity frontier
metrics.caveat: The paper treats the sparsity–fidelity frontier as necessary but not sufficient: small gains do not necessarily imply better representations or downstream interpretability performance. It reports other benchmark metrics alongside it.

metrics.name: Automated Interpretability
metrics.caveat: The paper notes that quantitative interpretability metrics may miss qualitative insights from manual investigation; it also cites that automated LLM judging can struggle to differentiate architectures.

metrics.name: k-Sparse Probing
metrics.caveat: The paper reports limited differentiation among architectures, widths, and sparsities, and notes prior findings that probe-based scores can be noisy. It evaluates k∈{1,2,5} and focuses analysis on k=1.

metrics.name: RAVEL
metrics.caveat: The paper notes that steering a few latents can change behavior even when a concept is distributed across many latents; it contrasts this with zero-ablation metrics as a stronger test of complete concept isolation. RAVEL averages Cause and Isolation metrics.

metrics.name: Feature Absorption
metrics.caveat: As a supervised metric, it is limited by the availability of ground-truth concepts, and the paper notes that limited supervised concepts can make some metrics noisy.

metrics.name: Unlearning Capability
metrics.caveat: Meaningful measurement requires adequate baseline task performance; Gemma-2-2B had sufficient performance on only one existing unlearning test set. MMLU categories are reported to check retained capabilities.

metrics.name: Spurious Correlation Removal (SCR)
metrics.caveat: As a supervised metric, it is limited by ground-truth concept availability; the paper notes that limited supervised concepts can make some metrics noisy. It reports scores across ablation sizes k∈{5,10,20,50,100,500}, focusing on k=20 and noting similar trends for k∈[5,50].

metrics.name: Targeted Probe Perturbation (TPP)
metrics.caveat: As a supervised metric, it is limited by ground-truth concept availability; the paper notes that limited supervised concepts can make some metrics noisy. It reports scores across ablation sizes k∈{5,10,20,50,100,500}, focusing on k=20 and noting similar trends for k∈[5,50].

controls.name: Random control sequences in Automated Interpretability
controls.detail: The test set includes random control sequences alongside sequences sampled to activate the selected latent at different activation strengths.
controls.rules_out: That the judge’s predictions are accurate merely because of properties shared by the test sequences, rather than because the feature description identifies latent-activating examples.

controls.name: MMLU retain-capability evaluation after unlearning
controls.detail: Evaluate MMLU categories alongside WMDP-bio unlearning performance to check that other capabilities are retained.
controls.rules_out: That apparent unlearning success is explained by broadly damaging model capabilities rather than selectively removing target-domain knowledge.

controls.name: SCR intervention-size sweep
controls.detail: Evaluate SCR across ablation set sizes k∈{5,10,20,50,100,500}, rather than only a fixed number of latents.
controls.rules_out: That worse SCR scaling for larger dictionaries is simply because a fixed intervention modifies a smaller fraction of the SAE.

confounds.name: Unlearning reflects general capability damage rather than selective knowledge removal
confounds.detail: Broadly degrading model performance could also reduce WMDP-bio accuracy, producing an apparent unlearning result.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Measure retained capabilities on MMLU categories alongside WMDP-bio test accuracy.

confounds.name: SCR inverse scaling is caused by modifying a smaller fraction of larger dictionaries
confounds.detail: A fixed number of ablated latents is a smaller fraction of a larger SAE, which could explain lower SCR scores without worse concept isolation.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Measure SCR across a range of intervention sizes; the inverse-scaling pattern persists for non-hierarchical architectures.

confounds.name: Differences in supervised-metric results across models reflect model capability, not SAE quality
confounds.detail: The paper says supervised metrics assume robust concepts such as spelling, professions, and demographics, which may be weaker in smaller models; patterns differ between Pythia-160M and Gemma-2-2B.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Compare results across Pythia-160M and Gemma-2-2B; the paper focuses main comparisons on Gemma-2-2B because it better represents real-world usage and supports the supervised concepts more robustly.

confounds.name: Apparent architecture gains are due to different sparsity levels rather than improved performance
confounds.detail: Many evaluations correlate strongly with sparsity, so architecture differences could reflect different L0 values rather than a genuine improvement.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The practitioner guidance recommends evaluating multiple sparsities and checking whether a method advances the Pareto frontier on target metrics rather than relying on a single sparsity point.

evidence_standards.name: Compare across sparsities and require Pareto-frontier improvement
evidence_standards.detail: The paper recommends training multiple SAEs across L0∈[20,200] with directly comparable baselines; it says this helps distinguish genuine improvements from statistical noise or sparsity correlations and checks whether the method advances the Pareto frontier. Metrics are described as deterministic and reproducible. No seeds, variance estimates, confidence intervals, or statistical tests are specified.

datasets.name: CE-Bench contrastive story-pair dataset
datasets.eval_protocol: 5,000 pairs across 1,000 subjects (five pairs per subject), generated with GPT-4.1; for each story, average SAE activations across tokens, min-max normalize the contrastive and independence vectors, max-pool each, and combine them with sparsity using α=0.25 for the final score. Used to evaluate pretrained SAEs; no data split is specified.

datasets.name: SAE-Bench
datasets.eval_protocol: Published SAE-Bench interpretability scores are the reference for alignment on a validation testbed of 48 pretrained SAEs. Alignment is measured with CRPR, Spearman correlation, and Pearson correlation. A disjoint inference-only testbed of 45 SAEs has no publicly available SAE-Bench scores.

controls.name: C+I score without sparsity penalty
controls.detail: The paper compares the sum of contrastive and independence scores with the sparsity-aware score C+I−0.25*S on the validation testbed.
controls.rules_out: Shows whether adding the sparsity penalty improves alignment with SAE-Bench, rather than attributing the improvement to the contrastive and independence scores alone.

confounds.name: GPT-generated stories may favor models that capture GPT-4.1 stylistic and semantic regularities rather than broader linguistic patterns
confounds.detail: The paper acknowledges this as a possible bias in its headline evaluation.

confounds.name: The synthetic narrative dataset's limited domain coverage may make results fail to generalize to varied or domain-specific contexts
confounds.detail: The paper acknowledges that its 5,000 contrastive story pairs mainly cover synthetic narrative text and that generalizability is uncertain.

baselines.name: Claude Sonnet 3.5
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on intruder detection for the same 56 latents; the paper reports 50 prompts for Claude in the human comparison and 100 prompts for LLMs in the evaluator-correlation results.

baselines.name: Llama 3.1 70b
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared as an intruder-detection evaluator on the same task; the evaluator-correlation results use 100 prompts per latent.

baselines.name: Llama 3.1 8b
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared as an intruder-detection evaluator on the same task; the evaluator-correlation results use 100 prompts per latent.

baselines.name: QwQ 32b
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared as an intruder-detection evaluator on the same task; the evaluator-correlation results use 100 prompts per latent.

baselines.name: Gemini Flash 2.0
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared as an intruder-detection evaluator on the same task; the evaluator-correlation results use 100 prompts per latent.

metrics.name: Intruder detection accuracy
metrics.caveat: Accuracy varies with the activation decile used for examples; the paper reports accuracy for individual deciles as well as the average across deciles.

metrics.name: AUROC
metrics.caveat: For example embedding scoring, scores are often close to chance, and the paper says the embedding model may miss the highlighted activating token and attend to context as a whole; it reports results across deciles and compares them with human and LLM intruder scores.

confounds.name: Most latents are binary and monosemantic, so examples from different activation deciles should not be distinguishable
confounds.detail: If this account were true, strong intruder-decile detection could be explained without latents encoding scalar or intensity-related distinctions.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper runs an intruder-decile task in which all examples activate the same latent and one comes from a different decile; accuracy is above chance for many majority/intruder decile pairs, which the authors use to rule out that most features are both binary and monosemantic.

confounds.name: LLMs may detect convoluted activation patterns that humans cannot understand
confounds.detail: High LLM intruder-detection scores could then overstate human interpretability.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Compare LLM and human scores on the same latents and task: the paper reports score correlations and binned-score agreement, and observes that humans mostly rate latents as more interpretable than the LLM.

confounds.name: Example embedding scores may reflect surrounding context rather than the highlighted activating token
confounds.detail: The embedding model may therefore score examples without capturing the feature-specific evidence relevant to interpretability.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Not ruled out. The authors acknowledge this as a weakness and suggest it helps explain the lower correlation of example embedding scores with human intruder scores.

evidence_standards.name: Intruder-task chance level and interpretability bins
evidence_standards.detail: For the five-example task, random guessing is 20%; the paper treats accuracy at or below 20% as clearly uninterpretable and divides higher scores into four 20-percentage-point interpretability bins.

evidence_standards.name: Human and LLM prompt counts for evaluator comparisons
evidence_standards.detail: Humans saw about 10–20 prompts per latent on average; Claude Sonnet 3.5 was evaluated on 50 prompts for the direct human comparison, and LLMs on 100 prompts per latent for evaluator correlations.

evidence_standards.name: Inter-human agreement study
evidence_standards.detail: Two human labelers evaluated a smaller set of 40 latents, with 3–5 prompts per latent; the paper reports their correlation.

datasets.name: Wikipedia articles
datasets.eval_protocol: Training data consists of 1 billion residual-stream vectors from layer 20 of Gemma 2-2B, collected from the first 256 tokens of articles spanning multiple languages and topics. Vectors are normalized to unit norm; no mean is subtracted and no bias term is used. All models are trained on this data for 4 epochs. For the cross-language redundancy evaluation, 1,000 English sequences of 16–48 tokens are sampled from the training data and translated into French, Spanish, and German with Gemini-2.0-Flash; the top 8 features on each translation’s last token are compared.

datasets.name: SAEBench first-letter classification benchmark
datasets.eval_protocol: Run the first-letter classification task while increasing the number of features used above 1. Report the fraction of the probe projection not explained by a single feature; the task should require only one feature if there is no splitting or absorption.

baselines.name: TopK SAE (Gao et al., 2024)
baselines.fair_comparison: All models are trained on the same data for 4 epochs; comparisons are shown across dictionary sizes.

metrics.name: LLM cross-entropy loss induced by reconstructed activations
First-letter classification absorption (fraction of probe projection not explained by a single feature)
metrics.caveat: The paper notes that general-purpose automated interpretability evaluations can be misleading, particularly for abstract features; it focuses on feature splitting and absorption as more measurable aspects and also reports feature visualizations and cross-language redundancy.

metrics.name: Symmetric set difference between top-8 feature sets across languages

confounds.name: Reconstruction gains could come at the cost of interpretability
confounds.detail: A modification can improve reconstruction while sacrificing interpretability, so better reconstruction alone would not establish an improved reconstruction–interpretability frontier.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Compare feature visualizations and evaluate feature absorption with the SAEBench first-letter classification benchmark, and feature redundancy across translated versions of the same sequences using symmetric set differences between top-8 feature sets.

datasets.name: SynthSAEBench-16k
datasets.eval_protocol: Standard configuration: 16,384 features in hidden dimension 768, with L0=34 synthetic activations. SAEs are width 4,096 and trained on 200M samples with batch size 1,024; the main comparison varies SAE L0 from 15 to 45 and uses 5 seeds per L0. The paper does not specify an evaluation split or evaluation-set size. Logistic-regression probe results are for the 4,096 highest-frequency features; further training/evaluation details are referred to Appendix L.

baselines.name: Standard L1 SAE
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared with the other SAE architectures at width 4,096 on 200M samples, across the same target L0 values and 5 seeds; its sparsity coefficient is automatically tuned to hit the target L0.

baselines.name: Matching Pursuit SAE
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared with the other SAE architectures at width 4,096 on 200M samples, across the same target L0 values and 5 seeds.

baselines.name: BatchTopK SAE
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared with the other SAE architectures at width 4,096 on 200M samples, across the same target L0 values and 5 seeds.

baselines.name: Matryoshka BatchTopK SAE
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared with the other SAE architectures at width 4,096 on 200M samples, across the same target L0 values and 5 seeds.

baselines.name: JumpReLU SAE
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared with the other SAE architectures at width 4,096 on 200M samples, across the same target L0 values and 5 seeds; its sparsity coefficient is automatically tuned to hit the target L0.

metrics.name: Explained variance (R²) / variance explained
metrics.caveat: High reconstruction performance can coexist with poor feature recovery; the paper reports MCC and probing metrics alongside it. In the superposition ablation, Matching Pursuit improves reconstruction while MCC and F1 decline.

metrics.name: Precision
metrics.caveat: The paper reports a precision–recall trade-off as L0 changes: increasing L0 raises recall at the cost of precision; it reports recall and F1 alongside precision.

metrics.name: Recall
metrics.caveat: The paper reports a precision–recall trade-off as L0 changes: increasing L0 raises recall at the cost of precision; it reports precision and F1 alongside recall.

metrics.name: F1 score
metrics.caveat: F1 does not by itself show the precision–recall trade-off mediated by L0; the paper reports precision and recall separately.

controls.name: Varying superposition via hidden dimension
controls.detail: The authors vary the synthetic model hidden dimension from 256 to 1,536, scale training samples by (D/768)^0.6, and train all SAEs at L0=25.
controls.rules_out: Whether the Matching Pursuit reconstruction result is independent of superposition; the comparison isolates how changing superposition relates to reconstruction and feature-recovery metrics.

controls.name: Synthetic-data parameter ablations
controls.detail: The paper reports ablations of feature-correlation strength and rank, base firing probabilities, firing-magnitude standard deviation, and hierarchy depth.
controls.rules_out: Whether the reported architectural pattern is limited to the standard synthetic configuration; the paper says the overall pattern persists across these ablations.

confounds.name: Matching Pursuit reconstruction gains reflect fitting superposition noise rather than recovering features
confounds.detail: The high explained-variance result could look like better SAE performance even if the SAE does not recover ground-truth features.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Compare explained variance with MCC and probing F1 across hidden dimensions: as superposition increases, Matching Pursuit explained variance rises while MCC and F1 fall, indicating reconstruction gains without corresponding feature recovery.

confounds.name: Matryoshka SAEs’ low-L0 performance drop is caused by dead latents rather than an inherent architectural limitation
confounds.detail: The low-L0 drop could otherwise be interpreted as a fundamental weakness of the Matryoshka architecture.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper examines dead latents in Appendix H and introduces a per-prefix Matryoshka auxiliary loss that reduces, but does not eliminate, them.

evidence_standards.name: 5 seeds per L0; shaded standard deviation
evidence_standards.detail: The main L0-sweep results use 5 seeds per L0 and show standard deviation as shaded areas. The paper specifies no statistical test or numerical threshold for calling a difference real.

datasets.name: TracrBench
datasets.eval_protocol: Use 20 of the 121 programs as prompt examples and evaluate on the remaining 101. Sample up to five attempts per task; a program counts as correct only if it passes all five verification stages: compilation and execution, output correctness, Tracr validation, transformer compilation, and compiled-transformer correctness. Output checks use 1,000 random input-output pairs per program, with input lengths from 1 to 10. Report pass rate and a difficulty-weighted score based on the number of RASP functions.

baselines.name: Python program generation
baselines.fair_comparison: Generate Python programs for the same target algorithms and evaluate them on the same 101-item test set.

baselines.name: gpt-3.5-turbo-0125
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on the same 101-item test set; prompt variants are evaluated, with generation sampled at temperature 0.9 and top-p 0.95, using best-of-5 sampling.

baselines.name: gpt-4-turbo-2024-04-09
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on the same 101-item test set; prompt variants are evaluated, with generation sampled at temperature 0.9 and top-p 0.95, using best-of-5 sampling.

baselines.name: gpt-4o-2024-05-13
baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated on the same 101-item test set with the full prompt, at temperature 0.9 and top-p 0.95, using best-of-5 sampling.

baselines.name: claude-3-haiku-20240307
baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated on the same 101-item test set with the full prompt, at temperature 0.9 and top-p 0.95, using best-of-5 sampling.

baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated on the same 101-item test set with the full prompt, at temperature 0.9 and top-p 0.95, using best-of-5 sampling.

baselines.name: claude-3-opus-20240229
baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated on the same 101-item test set with the full prompt, at temperature 0.9 and top-p 0.95, using best-of-5 sampling.

baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated on the same 101-item test set with the full prompt, at temperature 0.9 and top-p 0.95, using best-of-5 sampling.

metrics.name: Pass rate
metrics.caveat: Does not account for differences in program difficulty; the paper reports a difficulty-weighted score alongside it.

controls.name: Zero-shot prompt
controls.detail: For GPT-3.5-turbo-0125 and GPT-4-turbo-2024-04-09, evaluate without RASP program examples in the prompt.
controls.rules_out: That performance with example-containing prompts reflects performance that would occur without examples.

controls.name: One-shot prompt
controls.detail: For GPT-3.5-turbo-0125 and GPT-4-turbo-2024-04-09, evaluate with one RASP program example in the prompt.
controls.rules_out: That the observed prompt-performance difference requires the full 20 examples rather than fewer examples.

confounds.name: General programming ability rather than RASP-specific ability
confounds.detail: High or low performance on RASP generation could reflect the model's general ability to program, rather than its ability to use RASP.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Evaluate Python program generation for the same target algorithms; the paper reports Python pass rate alongside RASP pass rate.

confounds.name: Unequal task difficulty drives pass-rate differences
confounds.detail: A pass rate could look low because successes are concentrated on easier programs, rather than reflecting performance across the range of task difficulty.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Report a difficulty-weighted score that weights successes by the number of RASP functions in each program.

evidence_standards.name: Best-of-5 sampling with fixed decoding settings
evidence_standards.detail: Allow up to five attempts per task, sampled from scratch; report results with temperature 0.9 and top-p 0.95. The paper does not report seeds, variance estimates, or statistical tests.

datasets.name: 1D elementary cellular automata (V=2, k=3)
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluate on rules held out from training; deterministic test and validation rule pools are mutually disjoint from training. For stochastic evaluation, draw a fresh rule by sampling each transition row independently from Dirichlet(1,...,1). Rejection-sample each trajectory so every neighborhood configuration appears in the T0 context rows; score cells from t=T0 through T−1. Report deterministic teacher-forced and greedy autoregressive accuracy, and stochastic temperature-1 autoregressive accuracy and KL.

datasets.name: 1D cellular automata (V=3, k=3)
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluate on rules held out from training; deterministic test and validation rule pools are mutually disjoint from training. For stochastic evaluation, draw a fresh rule by sampling each transition row independently from Dirichlet(1,...,1). Rejection-sample each trajectory so every neighborhood configuration appears in the T0 context rows; score cells from t=T0 through T−1. Report deterministic teacher-forced and greedy autoregressive accuracy, and stochastic temperature-1 autoregressive accuracy and KL.

datasets.name: 2D von Neumann cellular automata (V=2, k=5)
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluate on rules held out from training; deterministic test and validation rule pools are mutually disjoint from training. For stochastic evaluation, draw a fresh rule by sampling each transition row independently from Dirichlet(1,...,1). Rejection-sample each trajectory so every neighborhood configuration appears in the T0 context rows; score cells from t=T0 through T−1. Report deterministic teacher-forced and greedy autoregressive accuracy, and stochastic temperature-1 autoregressive accuracy and KL.

metrics.name: Stochastic autoregressive cell accuracy
metrics.caveat: The ceiling is well below 1; the paper also reports the posterior-predictive k-gram sampling baseline, which independently samples cells from the add-one-smoothed k-gram posterior predictive.

metrics.name: Autoregressive KL, D_KL(q_kgram || q_model)
metrics.caveat: Computed between predictive distributions on the model’s own autoregressive rollout; the paper reports it alongside stochastic autoregressive cell accuracy.

metrics.name: Mean attention mass on construction-predicted positions
K-gram predictive probe score
metrics.caveat: Defined as 1 minus the probe KL divided by the KL from the uniform distribution; the paper reports it alongside the configuration probe results.

controls.name: Random-cell attention-mask control
controls.detail: At evaluation, mask attention to the same number of randomly selected cells as in the routing-cell or matching-precedent mask condition.
controls.rules_out: That the accuracy drop is explained merely by masking attention to an equal number of cells.

controls.name: No-ablation condition
controls.detail: Evaluate without masking attention, alongside the routing-cell and matching-precedent masking conditions.
controls.rules_out: Provides the unablated reference for whether masking the theory-predicted positions reduces accuracy.

confounds.name: Accuracy reduction is due to generic attention masking, not reliance on the predicted routing or matching cells
confounds.detail: Masking any cells might reduce accuracy, making a drop after masking theory-predicted positions insufficient evidence that the model relies on those positions.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Compare against evaluation-time masks of the same number of randomly selected cells; these random controls have little effect while masking predicted routing cells or matching precedents reduces accuracy.

evidence_standards.name: Deterministic decoding conditions
evidence_standards.detail: Report cell accuracy under teacher forcing and under greedy autoregressive rollout.

evidence_standards.name: Stochastic decoding condition
evidence_standards.detail: Report autoregressive cell accuracy for temperature-1 rollouts.
